content.text: {"obligations": {"reduction": {"status": "written_and_valid", "quote": null, "witness": null, "load_bearing": null}, "lower_bound": {"status": "written_but_invalid", "quote": "We use the following elementary infinite sunflower fact: every infinite family of distinct finite sets has an infinite subfamily $X_{i_1},X_{i_2},\\ldots$ for which there is a fixed set $R$ satisfying", "witness": "COUNTEREXAMPLE to the quoted fact: the chain $\\{1\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,2,3\\},\\dots$ is an infinite family of distinct finite sets, but every infinite subfamily is a chain $X_{n_1}\\subsetneq X_{n_2}\\subsetneq X_{n_3}$, so $X_{n_1}\\cap X_{n_2}=X_{n_1}\\ne X_{n_2}=X_{n_2}\\cap X_{n_3}$; no fixed core $R$ exists. The sketched induction (\"delete that element and continue\") only closes when set sizes are bounded. Consequently Lemma 1 itself, as stated, is false: take $X_n=\\{1,\\dots,n-1,c_n\\}$ ($n\\ge 2$, $c_n$ distinct new elements) and $\\mathcal A=\\{X_2,X_3,\\dots\\}$, which is pairwise intersecting since $1\\in X_n$ for all $n$. For each $k\\ge 2$ the set $T_k=\\{k,c_2,\\dots,c_k\\}$ is a transversal (it meets $X_n$ via $c_n$ for $n\\le k$ and via $k$ for $n\\ge k+1$) and is minimal (dropping $k$ misses $X_{k+1}$; dropping $c_j$ misses $X_j$). So $\\mathcal A$ has infinitely many inclusion-minimal finite transversals, contradicting Lemma 1.
